title: Eleven Senate Seats Most Likely to Flip as US Midterms Reach Election Eve
excerpt: CNN's final ranking puts North Carolina, Ohio and Texas at the top, adds South Carolina at the last minute, and leaves Democrats needing four Republican seats plus a clean defense to take the majority.
body:
• CNN's final ranking lists 11 Senate seats as plausible flips, and Democrats need to gain four Republican-held seats while holding all of their own to win the majority.
  • North Carolina is rated the likeliest flip, followed by Ohio and Texas; South Carolina joined the list for the first time in the final update.
  • President Trump's approval rating sits at 34% in CNN's Poll of Polls, and Republicans outspent Democrats $560 million to $521 million in the final month across the 11 races, per AdImpact.
  • Polls close Tuesday, November 3; Alaska's ranked-choice count could take weeks, so Senate control may not be known on election night.

One day before the midterm elections, CNN has expanded its ranking of Senate seats most likely to flip to 11, adding South Carolina after late polling showed a tied race in a state Donald Trump won by 18 points in 2024. Democrats appear within reach of the majority, CNN reports, but most of the seats in play are toss-ups in deep-red states. To take the Senate, Democrats must flip four Republican-held seats and defend every seat they hold, including Michigan and Georgia.

The top of the list

1. North Carolina. Former Democratic governor Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley; a final High Point University/YouGov poll put Cooper up 14 points among likely voters, though CNN cautions the actual margin is not expected to be that wide. Republicans have pulled back spending, with Democrats outspending them $10.4 million to $2.5 million in the last two weeks.

2. Ohio. CNN's Poll of Polls average has former senator Sherrod Brown leading Republican Senator Jon Husted 50% to 45%. Ohio's governor's race matters to the diaspora too: Republican nominee Vivek Ramaswamy has trailed Democrat Amy Acton in recent polls, per CNN.

3. Texas. Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton show no clear leader in CNN's Poll of Polls average, though two late polls put Talarico ahead outside the margin of error. Texas has already cast 7.7 million early ballots, the most of any state.

4. Maine. Democrat Troy Jackson leads Republican Senator Susan Collins 50% to 46% in CNN's Poll of Polls average. Collins, running for a sixth term, is the only Republican incumbent on the ballot in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024.

The red-state gambles

5. Alaska. A New York Times/Siena poll showed no clear leader between Democrat Mary Peltola and Senator Dan Sullivan, 48% to 46%. A same-name ballot controversy, now under state and federal investigation, adds uncertainty, and ranked-choice counting means the result may take weeks.

6. Kansas. Democrat Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, led Senator Roger Marshall 49% to 44% in a New York Times/Siena poll. Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932; Democratic groups outspent Republicans $45.7 million to $31.5 million in October.

7. Iowa. No clear leader in the open-seat race to succeed Senator Joni Ernst: Democrat Josh Turek at 46% and Republican Representative Ashley Hinson at 45% in CNN's average, with farm-state anger over diesel, fertilizer and tariff costs in play.

8. Michigan. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers 50% to 45%, despite a late cross-party shock: Democratic Representative Haley Stevens endorsed Rogers on Sunday, a move Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called a betrayal. About 1.5 million early votes were already cast by Sunday.

The defensive holds

9. New Hampshire. Democrat Chris Pappas leads former Republican senator John Sununu by 12 points in a University of New Hampshire poll for the open seat.

10. South Carolina. The list's newest entry: a New York Times/Siena poll showed appointed Republican Senator Darline Graham, running for a full term after her brother Lindsey Graham's death in July, tied with Democrat Annie Andrews, who has out-raised her.

11. Georgia. Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, has out-raised and outpolled Republican Representative Mike Collins throughout; CNN says a Republican flip here now looks unlikely.

Nebraska, Mississippi and Minnesota sit on CNN's bubble; flips there would be a surprise. The full ranking and the state-by-state map are at CNN's final Senate rankings. For Indian-American voters, control of the Senate shapes the committees that handle immigration and trade legislation for the next two years, which is why these 11 races carry weight well beyond their states.
